label: US Unemployment Rate
deltaNote: July 2026 (Aug 7): NFP fell 23,000 — a sharp miss vs the ~83,000 gain expected — with May and June revised down a combined 103,000. Unemployment eased to 4.1%, largely on lower labor-force participation rather than underlying strength. Markets read the report as reducing Fed hike risk; S&P 500 closed at a record high same day.

label: US PCE Inflation (May 2026 — Highest Since 2023)
deltaNote: MAY 2026 (released June 25): Headline PCE 4.1% YoY (+0.4% MoM) — highest since April 2023. Core PCE 3.4% YoY (vs 3.3% forecast). Personal income and spending each +0.7% MoM; saving rate held at 3%. Released just over a week after Warsh's hawkish dot plot, complicating the disinflation narrative even as Iran-deal oil relief began working through the data. June CPI (July 14) subsequently cooled to 3.5%, suggesting May PCE may mark the cycle high.

label: Michigan Consumer Sentiment (May 2026 Final)
deltaNote: MAY 2026 FINAL — THIRD CONSECUTIVE ALL-TIME RECORD LOW: 44.8 shatters April's 47.6 record (already below 1980 energy crisis nadir of 51.7). Preliminary reading was 48.2; final collapsed 3.4 points — unusually large revision. Year-ahead inflation expectations: 4.5% (down from April's 4.7% — the largest one-month jump in survey history). ~1/3 of respondents spontaneously mentioned gasoline prices; ~30% mentioned tariffs. Deepest consumer pessimism in the survey's 70+ year history. S&P 500 closed 8 consecutive weekly gains (7,473.47); the sentiment/spending divergence has never been wider.

label: Global Policy Uncertainty / Recession Risk
value: AUG 10: Fed Held Jul 29 (3.50-3.75%, 3 Hawkish Dissents); Section 301 Tariffs (10-12.5%) Live Since Jul 24; Jul NFP -23K Shock; S&P Record Close; Brent Round-Tripped $100→$90s
source: Federal Reserve / BEA / BLS / ISM / Eurostat; July 17 – August 10, 2026
delta: JULY 23-AUG 10 ARC — OIL SHOCK, TARIFF CLIFF RESOLVES, JOBS SHOCK REVERSES HIKE FEARS: Houthi tanker attacks off Saudi Arabia reflared the Hormuz/Red Sea oil shock July 23, sending Brent above $100 and September Fed-hike odds to ~82% intraday. The Section 122 tariff surcharge expired by statute July 24, replaced same-minute by Section 301 forced-labor tariffs (10-12.5%) on 60 economies — the coverage gap traders had worried about did not materialize. The FOMC held rates July 29 despite the inflation scare, with 3 members dissenting in favor of a hike. Q2 GDP's advance estimate (July 30, +1.5%) missed the 2.1% forecast, and China's Politburo (July 31) pledged only targeted stimulus. Eurozone inflation rose to 2.9% (July 31) on the oil shock. ISM prints were mixed: manufacturing surged to 55.6% (Aug 3, best since May 2022) while services' employment sub-index fell into contraction (Aug 5). The July jobs report (Aug 7: NFP -23K, May/June revised down 103K combined) reversed the hawkish repricing entirely — the S&P 500 closed at a record high and Fed September hike odds collapsed.
deltaNote: AUG 10 RECESSION RISK SNAPSHOT: The dominant swing factor this window was geopolitical-energy, not domestic demand — the Jul 23 Hormuz/Red Sea tanker attacks pushed Brent through $100 and briefly repriced Fed policy toward a hike, before the Aug 7 jobs miss flipped sentiment back toward a hold/cut bias. Growth signals are genuinely mixed: GDP advance missed, ISM manufacturing hit a 4-year high, ISM services employment contracted, and payrolls swung negative with large downward revisions. The tariff transition (Section 122 → Section 301) executed without the feared coverage gap. Next catalysts: August CPI, the September FOMC, and whether China's 'targeted' stimulus pledge translates into concrete measures.

label: BOJ Policy Rate
source: Bank of Japan, June 16 2026 (25bp hike — highest since 1995)
deltaNote: June 16: BOJ hiked 25bp to 1.00%, the highest level since 1995, in a 7-1 vote (Asada dissenting) — citing Iran-war energy-cost pass-through risk. The hike landed the same day Warsh's first FOMC opened, raising August-2024-style carry-unwind concerns; the immediate market reaction was orderly (Nikkei +0.46%), but the yen still fell to a fresh 40-year low past 162/USD by June 30 despite the hike and an estimated $72.5bn in prior FX intervention.
